newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ bonds, bills sell off at Tuesday's close.
newsitem.headline: NZ bonds, bills sell off at Tuesday's close.

text.p: Figures in brackets compare against previous day's close
FUTURES PHYSICAL YIELD
OVERNIGHT CASH 9.35 PCT (PREV 9.35) US 30-YR 6.51 (PREV 6.51)
* NZ bonds, bills sell off at close
* NZ First's Peters knocks confidence
* Potential for further selling if demand not found
New Zealand bonds sold off five to six basis points at Tuesday's close as a fairly thin market reacted to comments by New Zealand First leader Winston Peters.

Three and 10-year bond yields climbed five and six basis points respectively on the day, while 90-day bank bills ended on their opening level of 9.20 percent. The December futures contract was five points weaker at 91.20.

Dealers said there has been little other domestic information to trade off, especially given the secrecy surrounding coalition negotiations in the bid to form a new government after October's inconclusive general election.

Peters called a question-and-answer session with journalists at late notice. He said there was a "certain inevitability" about the new government widening the Reserve Bank's 0-2 percent inflation target band.

Peters also said the economy was in a worse state than the caretaker conservative National party was arguing before the election. New Zealand First holds the balance of power after the election and is negotiating with both Labour and National on coalition possibilities.
"It's just a small loss of confidence, I think," one dealer said.

"Nothing has been said that wasn't already known, but people were just reminded of it, that maybe they had ignored politics too much -- you get a statement like that a little bit out of the blue, and it's like the honeymoon is over."
Dealers said the impact of recent eurokiwi issues on the shorter maturities had been limited.

"The 7/98s were being used to hedge those, and the 7/98s are no longer special. I presume people are now hedging by finding a swaps payer in New Zealand -- with the swaps rate at 7.5 percent for a forward start, there is no problem in finding New Zealand companies, banks, individuals or whatever, willing to buy fixed rate at 7.5 percent for two or three years," one dealer said.
He said the session's sell-off was significant in that it left New Zealand bonds at a spread of some 105 points over U.S.

"It will be quite a test to see whether or not there is actually demand for New Zealand bonds at these levels. If we don't find buying demand, then the market is set up to sell a little bit more. Not in leaps and bounds though -- another five basis points or so," he said.
